common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: No source gives a tested way to tell the causes apart, or says which is most common (R-1). Sources disagree on sun hours (C-1), on feeding (C-2), on where to cut a blind shoot (C-4), on first-season flowering (C-5), on how hard is too hard (C-6) and on chemical treatment of balling (C-7). Rose midge has no New Zealand or Australian source (R-3). Lower-confidence findings (potassium AF-7, heat AF-9, cold AF-10, hips AF-20, rootstock AF-32, pesticides AF-33) are not used in this answer.

items.text: I can't tell you which reason applies to your rose. Here are the common reasons, with what to look for and what helps.
Too little sun, or too much shade, means fewer flowers.
Roses need at least four to eight hours of direct sun a day. Six is the figure most often given.
Tree roots and nearby shrubs compete with a rose for water and food. Plant roses away from them.
Too much fertiliser, especially nitrogen, gives lots of leafy growth and few flowers.
Too little feeding can also mean fewer flowers, and feeding helps.
Too little water, or drought, can reduce flowering. A rose short of water may drop leaves and make small flowers. Pale, limp leaves can also come from afternoon heat.
Pruning too hard, too little or at the wrong time can mean fewer flowers. I couldn't find how much pruning is too much; a local rose society can help.
Harder pruning gives fewer, larger flowers. Lighter pruning gives more, smaller ones.
Removing spent flowers from a repeat-flowering rose encourages more flowers.

If your rose flowered once in late spring or early summer and not again, it may be a once-flowering variety. I can't support those yet. A local rose society or garden centre can help, or you can check its type with my rose-type questions.
Pruning a once-flowering rose before it flowers removes its flowers.
A blind shoot grows and leafs normally but has no flower bud at its tip.
The cause of blind shoots isn't known. Sources suggest weather, shade, over-feeding and big swings between day and night temperatures.

Cut a blind shoot back so it can send up a new shoot that flowers later in the season. Sources disagree on where to cut: one cuts it back by about half, to a strong bud; another cuts to the next leaf joint down.
One source says buds that form but don't open after cool, wet weather may be "balled": the outer petals dry into a brown, papery shell.
Remove balled buds promptly, before grey mould sets in. One source also suggests better air flow around the plant and watering at the base, not over the leaves.
Spotted petals with grey fuzz may point to grey mould (botrytis), which is more common in cool, wet weather.
Brown or white streaks on petals, or distorted flowers, may point to thrips (tiny insects that feed on flowers).
Holes in buds, with caterpillars, may point to budworm (caterpillars that feed on buds).
Black spot (dark spots on the leaves, then yellowing and leaf drop) can weaken a rose. Repeated severe leaf loss means fewer, poorer flowers.
A photo alone can't show why a rose isn't flowering. Check these signs on the plant itself.
